entries.title: Man fatally stabbed during fight in Calumet Heights
entries.summary: <p>A man is dead after being stabbed during a fight in Calumet Heights Wednesday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, whose age wasn’t known, was involved in an altercation with someone near the 1400 block of East 87th Street at 6:54 p.m. when he was stabbed multiple times, police said. The wounded man was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where he later died.</p><p>No one is in custody, police said. An investigation is ongoing.</p>

entries.title: White Sox burn both ABS challenges in third inning of Game 3 ALDS loss to Guardians
entries.summary: <p>The White Sox have maintained all year that empowering their players to be aggressive with ABS challenges of umpires’ ball-and-strike calls will pay larger dividends on balance, even if it entails some nights where the club burns through both their ABS challenges in short order.</p><p>They probably hoped such a scenario didn't take place in the third inning of Game 3 of the American League Division Series, as catcher <b>Kyle Teel</b>–who had been 7-for-8 in the postseason entering Wednesday–lost both ABS challenges in successive plate appearances while trying to guide a wild <b>Bryan Hudson</b> through a disastrous, four-run frame.</p><p>“I felt good, he put a good swing on it,” said <b>Hagen Smith</b>, who relieved Hudson but yielded a bases-clearing triple to <b>Jo Adell </b>that put two more runs on Hudson’s tab.</p><p>Did the lack of challenges contribute to an ugly afternoon where the White Sox lost the battle of the strike zone, with their pitchers issuing 10 walks and their hitters punching out 19 times? It didn’t help, but it would be hard for the ABS system to carry that much weight.</p><p>“Just need to be better,” said Teel. “Bad game for me [with] challenging. Learn from it, do better tomorrow, but it’s got to be better.”</p><p>The Sox further lost a replay challenge in the bottom of the fourth, immediately after the Guardians successfully challenged that left-hander <b>Foster Griffin</b>’s pitch did not hit <b>Tristan Peters</b> in the hand but instead hit his bat. Sox manager <b>Will Venable </b>countered by challenging that<b> </b>catcher <b>Patrick Bailey </b>had committed catcher’s interference on Peters’ check-swing, but to no avail.</p><p>This all took place in the second pitch of the at-bat, before Peters eventually doubled home <b>Chase Meidroth </b>on the ninth.</p><p><b>Antonacci did his part</b></p><p>White Sox rookie <b>Sam Antonacci</b> usually defines his job on offense as just getting on base, especially when facing fellow left-handers. It’s hard to quibble with his work in a losing effort on Wednesday.</p><p>Antonacci’s only hit came on a medium-speed ground ball up the middle off lefty <b>Joey Cantillo</b>. Yet he reached base four times, including scoring after a leadoff walk in the first. The other two times? You’re supposed to lean on your strengths in the postseason, and MLB’s hit-by-pitch leader was plunked twice in Game 3, including to force home a run with the bases loaded in the sixth.</p><p><b>Playoff atmosphere</b></p><p>A mistake-filled blowout loss did not put White Sox players in an especially reflective mood about fan support, but there are only so many chances to play in front of 40,590 screaming fans dressed in all black.</p><p>“To be real honest, I was a little emotional,” said right-hander <b>Davis Martin</b>, the team’s longest-tenured player. “National anthem, like just seeing it all and experiencing what we went through in [2024], and just to get back to this point was unbelievable.”</p><p>The Sox will be leaning on fan support again on Thursday, with another chance to clinch a bid to the American League Championship Series.</p><p>“They’ve been amazing all year,” said Meidroth. “We wouldn’t have been in this spot without them and we’re looking forward to [Thursday].”</p><p><b>Scoreboard watching</b></p><p>With the Yankees down 2-0 and facing elimination in their ALDS matchup against the Rays, whether they can stay alive affects the White Sox’ Game 4 start time. Sox-Guardians is scheduled for 4pm CT, but will shift to 7pm if the Yankees lose.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: Will White Sox ever win a postseason series in Chicago? After losing Game 3, they're down to their last shot
entries.summary: <p>They’re dying to dance in the streets of Bridgeport and Armour Square, Back of the Yards and Beverly, Roseland and Hegewisch, Calumet Park and South Holland.</p><p>Oh, so ready to raise a glass at Bernice’s Tavern and Shinnick’s Pub, at Cork & Kerry and Jimmy’s Woodlawn Tap.</p><p>And to break bread with gleeful goodwill at Fat Johnnie’s, Vito & Nick’s, Valois, Daley’s and the Duck Inn.</p><p>For once, the South Side wants to see its beloved <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> clinch a postseason series in Chicago, something that hasn’t occurred since — if you can believe it — the 1906 World Series against the Cubs.</p><p>Those Cubs had a winning percentage of .763, still the highest in baseball’s modern era. Those Sox were so bad at swinging the sticks, they were known as the “Hitless Wonders.” The Sox won anyway, which, of course, not a damn one of us remembers.</p><p>But now there’s a division series against the Guardians, and a Sox team that arrived at Rate Field on Wednesday leading two games to none in a best-of-five.</p><p>A “Blackout” in the stands. Towels waving. Fans aroar. And — what a letdown — a 9-3 Sox defeat.</p><p>That leaves <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/chicago-white-sox-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-miguel-vargas-kyle-teel-chase-meidroth-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >one more shot Thursday for the Sox to clinch at home</a>. By God, it’s time for it to finally happen. The 1917 Sox won the World Series over the New York Giants at the Polo Grounds. The 2005 champs enjoyed clinchers in Boston, Anaheim and Houston. This year’s team swept the Astros in the wild-card round in Houston. The South Side needs a celebration.</p><p>Either that or win Game 5 back in Cleveland, but who wants to bet on that?</p><p>The odds remain in the Sox’ favor, for what it’s worth. Right around 90% of major league teams that have led 2-0 in best-of-five series have ended up happy.</p><p>But the Guardians are busting with confidence after getting off the schneid.</p><p>“I would say our confidence is at a 10 [out of 10],” said pitcher Gavin Williams, the American League’s strikeout champion, who would get the ball in Game 5 if he doesn’t appear in relief in Game 4 and the Guardians remain alive. “It better be a 10.”</p><p>The Sox will have to tangle again with the Guardians’ top starter this season, Parker Messick, in Game 4.</p><p>“I’m ready to rock and roll,” Messick said.</p><p>But the Sox are ready to frame and hang more newspaper pages in the Rate press box. Yes, newspapers still exist — don’t even joke about that — and dated ones mark all the biggest Sox occasions on the walls where the home and visiting scribes sit.</p><p>The Sun-Times cover pages alone are wonderful to see. “EL, YES!” in big, fat headline type after Orlando “El Duque” Hernandez pitched the Sox past the Red Sox in 2005. “WORLD CLASS” after the Sox got past the Angels that year. “CHAMPS!” after they won it all against the Astros. “SOXAPALOOZA!” after the downtown parade.</p><p>The press box is screaming for an image of the Sox piling onto the mound right here at home.</p><p>Jose Abreu didn’t win a postseason series here. Mark Buerhle, Frank Thomas, Harold Baines, Dick Allen, Luis Aparicio, Minnie Minoso, Nellie Fox — none of them. You get the picture.</p><p>What better time than now, when there are no paper bags over heads and no “Sell the team!” signs in the crowd?</p><p>The Sox are only the fourth team ever to appear in the postseason a year after losing 100 games, and they’re the one and only team to do so after losing 100 games back-to-back (or, in the Sox’ case, back-to-back-to-back). It’s still crazy that they’re even in this position, but they might as well not foul it up now, right?</p><p>Again, though, the Guardians, accustomed to being better than their division rivals, have their chests puffed out.</p><p>“We’ve got to stand on something,” said outfielder Steven Kwan, who drove in his team’s first run on a win-or-go-home late afternoon.</p><div class="Enhancement" and his glove. When he doubled to left, stole third and came flying home on an infield grounder in the fifth, beating second baseman Chase Meidroth’s throw, all the game’s momentum went with him.</p><p>“That made it a Jose Ramirez game,” Kwan said.</p><p>In the sixth, Ramirez made a diving stop of a Miguel Vargas smash with the bases loaded and two out and the Sox down just 5-3.</p><p>“After that I felt like, ‘This is going to be our game,’ ” Ramirez said via a translator.</p><p>It was game on. Now it’s series on.</p><p>“We came here to compete,” Ramirez said. “That’s what [the Sox] did when they weren’t at home. They won two games. We can do it, too.”</p><p>There’s a question Guardians manager Stephen Vogt often asks his team: “What do you like better, making 50,000 people go crazy or shutting 50,000 people up?”</p><p>One happens at home and the other on the road, of course.</p><p>“Both very different feelings,” Vogt said, “but they’re equally as fun.”</p><p>But nothing tops winning a postseason series on your home turf. The Sox and their fans wouldn’t know this, but they can ask around.</p><p>There’s one more shot at it. The headline awaits.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/10/07/chicago-white-sox-cleveland-guardians-will-venable-miguel-vargas-kyle-teel-chase-meidroth-mlb-playoffs-postseason" target="_blank" >White Sox believe in tomorrow — but there are only so many left</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: White Sox put on worst performance in weeks, in front of first home playoff crowd in years
entries.summary: <p>Will Venable’s ballclub proved him right on Wednesday in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, albeit not in a way he appreciated.</p><p>“Talked about this the whole series, that these guys are going to make you pay for walks,” Venable said postgame. “First couple games, they didn't. But today, they did.”</p><p>After defying that axiom in a rocky first inning of their Game 2 win in Cleveland, the Sox and 40,590 supporters were dragged back to reality in a 9-3 blowout loss in Game 3. Sox pitching issued 10 free passes (one intentional) to Guardians hitters, while their hitters struck out 19 times; an MLB postseason record for a nine-inning game</p><p>“They just controlled the zone well,” said catcher Kyle Teel.</p><p>The Sox walked eight Guardians hitters in two games in Cleveland, and actually only three in Game 2. But Bryan Hudson and Hagen Smith combined for three in a four-run third alone, capped off by a bases-clearing Jo Adell triple that put the Guardians up for good.</p><p>“Just the pitching staff as a whole, minimizing walks and leadoff walks,” said Davis Martin–who issued two himself in the ninth–when asked what was missing from the Sox effort. “That [the Guardians’] lineup in general. They work hard [at-bats], they know the zone.”</p><p>Venable’s pre-series warning applied to not just walks, but allowing stolen bases and defensive misplays. All free bases yielded to the opponent needed to be trimmed from their diet.</p><p>Instead, the first of two Guardians stolen bases led to a run, with Jose Ramirez nabbing third after a one-out double in the fifth, allowing him to score on a hard grounder to Chase Meidroth. Playing from behind and not in position to deploy their best outfield defenders, Ramirez’s two-run bloop triple dropped beyond Randal Grichuk’s dive to put things out of reach in the eighth, before Miguel Vargas lost track of Brayan Rocchio’s pop behind third base to plate another run in the ninth.</p><p>“A lot of times during the year we lost tough games, and we bounced back the next day,” said Vargas. “That’s what we do.”</p><p>The Sox had no losing streaks longer than four, no winning streaks longer than five this year. With four playoff wins after winning their regular season finale, maybe they hit their cap and were due for their worst performance in weeks, unfortunately during the first home playoff crowd at Rate Field in five years.</p><p>“This is what we’ve been doing all year,” said Sean Newcomb, the only Sox pitcher who didn’t issue a walk over his two scoreless innings as opener.</p><p>But the longer this series stretches on, the trickier it becomes for the White Sox to navigate the Guardians’ starting pitching advantage. It was on display even with both sides running bullpen games on Wednesday, as All-Star left-hander Foster Griffin worked in bulk and recorded a Guardians’ record seven strikeouts as a reliever, and the Sox bullpen saw their control abandon them amid weeks of heavy use.</p><p>Of the five Sox pitchers on the ALDS roster who didn’t pitch Wednesday, two are high-leverage relievers (Grant Taylor and Jordan Hicks), two are starters who have only appeared in relief so far (Anthony Kay and Erick Fedde) and one is pretty essential to any Game 5 plans (Sean Burke). True to form, the Sox have not announced a Game 4 starter as of press time, and will likely be piecing things together as they go, figuring out which arms are available during pre-game catch play.</p><p>For their part, the Guardians are starting likely AL Cy Young finalist Parker Messick on regular rest.</p><p>“We’ve seen him a lot, I think that helps and our gameplan against him will be similar,” said outfielder Tristan Peters. “We've been resilient the whole season. Why can't we do it now?”</p><p>No insurmountable reason comes to mind. But if they don’t, it’ll be hard to remember all the times they did.</p>
entries.author: James Fegan

entries.title: White Sox believe in tomorrow — but there are only so many left
entries.summary: <p>Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the mouth.</p><p>Heavyweight champ Mike Tyson spoke those words about 30 years ago, and they often proved prophetic after his opponent entered the ring. The man had 44 knockouts. That’s a lot of plans getting torn up.</p><p>For the first time this postseason, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> took a punch in the mouth. They suffered their first loss Wednesday, falling to the Guardians 9-3. After beating the Astros twice in the wild-card series and taking the first two in the division series, the Sox find themselves in a new position — having to bounce back from a playoff defeat.</p><p>When the Sox were knocked down in the regular season, they didn’t stay down long. Their longest losing streak was four games, and it took them until August to reach it. That was impressive, but they don’t have that kind of time here. The ref is starting his 10-count.</p><p>“We’ve done it all year,” manager Will Venable said. “We’ve been in tough spots where we haven’t played our best games, we’ve played good games. Whatever the result, these guys came back the next day. It’s really been the story of our group, being able to bounce back no matter what happens.”</p><p>What happened Wednesday was the Sox struck out 19 times. In case you forgot, a team gets 27 outs in baseball. That means the Sox didn’t put the ball in play nearly as much as they needed to. They had six hits.</p><p>The Sox can’t chase pitches Thursday in Game 4 against left-handed starter Parker Messick, who had 193 strikeouts in the regular season, tied for 15th in baseball. If they do, it won’t get any easier in Game 5. The Guardians have righty Gavin Williams, the American League strikeout leader with 248, lined up. Can the Sox beat either again?</p><p>But let’s focus on one crisis at a time. In fact, let’s take a deep breath and take a cue from the Sox, who are convinced they’ve been here before — even though they really haven’t.</p><p>“A lot of times during the year, we lost tough games, and we bounced back the next day,” third baseman Miguel Vargas said. “That’s what we do. We have a short memory, I guess. We’re going to be ready for tomorrow.”</p><p>“Today has nothing to do with tomorrow. Nothing,” catcher Kyle Teel said defiantly. “We come ready to go like we always do tomorrow.”</p><p>The Sox do have some things going for them. They didn’t need Grant Taylor and his mechanical right arm in Game 3. That means he’ll have a whole extra day of rest before Game 4 than he did before Game 2, when he earned the save just two days after pitching four innings to close out Game 1.</p><p>However, Taylor was shaky on the seven pitches he threw Monday. He gave Sox fans a palpitation on his first pitch, nearly allowing a game-tying home run to Jo Adell. His next pitch was a drive to deep left that was caught. Nursing a one-run lead in the ninth, he allowed back-to-back, scary-deep flies to center.</p><p>In 5 ⅓ innings this series, Taylor has allowed three hits and struck out six with no walks. But that outing could portend trouble.</p><p>Hagen Smith, the Sox’ other reliable reliever — or opener or whatever you want to call him — wasn’t so reliable Wednesday. Entering a 1-1 game in the third, he walked the first batter he faced, Jose Ramirez, to load the bases and was one strike away from getting out of trouble when Jo Adell tripled.</p><p>Smith hadn’t allowed a run in 5 ⅔ innings in the postseason, but he walked three in Game 1 against the Guardians. He said he could pitch Thursday, but he might need a break.</p><p>The Sox could have more trouble if Munetaka Murakami can’t rediscover his stroke from Cleveland, where he went 3-for-8 with a home run and three RBI. On Wednesday, the Guardians game-planned for him perfectly, having him face four pitchers, the last three of them lefties. He went 0-for-4 with three strikeouts.</p><p>That said, his home run in Game 1 came against Messick, whom the Sox knocked out in the fifth inning. See? It’s not all bad.</p><p>“It’s baseball. You’re not going to win every game,” second baseman Chase Meidroth said. “That’s the reality of it. But tomorrow is a new day; it’s a new game.”</p><p>That it is, but in a five-game series, there are only so many days left.</p>
